title: A Geometric Theory of Quantum Entanglement
authors: Lorenzo Capra, Lucio de Simone, Roberto Franzosi
abstract: Entanglement Distance (ED) was originally proposed as a geometric measure of entanglement derived from the Fubini-Study metric on the projective Hilbert space. Independently, the Meyer-Wallach and Scott measures quantify multipartite entanglement via linear entropy. In this work, we demonstrate that these two seemingly distinct frameworks are mathematically identical for pure states of arbitrary finite dimensions. We prove that ED arises naturally as the trace of the Fubini-Study metric tensor over the local subalgebra of observables. Crucially, this geometric unification yields a direct operational interpretation: the global entanglement of a pure state is exactly proportional to the total Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) available for local unitary estimation. This bridges abstract information geometry with quantum metrology, demonstrating that ED dynamically quantifies resourcefulness for distributed quantum sensing, identifying Heisenberg-limited sensitivity in regimes where standard variance-based witnesses fail.
summary: This paper unifies multiple entanglement measures—including Entanglement Distance (ED) and Quantum Fisher Information (QFI)—by showing they are all rooted in the geometry of the projective Hilbert space. It demonstrates that this geometric measure quantifies the total resourcefulness for local quantum sensing, providing a rigorous link between information geometry and quantum metrology.
main_problem: The paper aims to geometrically characterize and quantify quantum entanglement, establishing mathematical equivalences between various measures like Entanglement Distance (ED), Meyer-Wallach, and Quantum Fisher Information (QFI).
main_result: It proves that ED is mathematically equivalent to the sum of local linear entropies and is directly proportional to the total QFI available for local unitary estimation, bridging geometry and quantum metrology.
method: The analysis heavily utilizes the Fubini-Study metric on the projective Hilbert space and relates entanglement measures to the variance of local observable generators.
model_or_system: The work considers general finite-dimensional multipartite systems, analyzing specific dynamics using the Kitagawa-Ueda (KU) model for spin squeezing, and also examining the Haar-random state ensemble.
key_observables: Entanglement Distance (ED), Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), Spin Squeezing Parameter ($\xi^2$), and local linear entropies.
important_parameters: The number of qubits ($N$), time evolution parameter ($t$), and the local generator structure ($\mathfrak{su}(d_\mu)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the geometric approach is robust for extending measures to infinite-dimensional (CV) systems, though it notes a gap between theoretical saturation and experimental accessibility for random states.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the evolution of the Spin Squeezing Parameter ($\xi^2$), ED, and normalized Entropy of Entanglement for the KU Model, showing ED's distinct behavior.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the geometric framework using the Fubini-Study metric, derives the equivalence between ED and local entropy sums, applies this framework to the KU model to show metrological advantage, and finally analyzes the global average entanglement for Haar-random states.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, unified geometric tool (ED) that connects abstract concepts of entanglement to concrete, measurable quantities in quantum metrology (QFI), which is highly relevant for designing quantum sensing protocols.
